title: TimeTraveler: Temporal Strategy Planning with Time Dictionary for Streaming Video Understanding
claim: Prior memory methods use one lossy evidence-access path; ours plans the temporal strategy and queries a structured, recoverable dictionary.
layout: 3 stacked bands: timeline on top, prior then ours, left-to-right flow
description: The figure has three horizontal bands. The top band shows a video stream as a row of soccer-match frames along a timeline (t1 to t8), with a dashed query time tq and a question box. Braces label the regions as Past (green), Current (blue) and Future (orange). The middle gray band, 'Memory-based SVU', shows streamed frames feeding three boxed memory schemes: agent historical memory, pruned tokens, and KV-memory selective recall. To the right, a robot looks only at past frames ('Only Lookback'), with red ✗ marks beside 'Detail Memory Preservation?' and 'Temporal Planning?'. The bottom teal band, 'TimeTraveler (Ours)', flows left to right: the question context goes to a robot planner that says 'Looks past-related', then to three strategies (Past Lookback, Current Perception, Future Observation). These access a Time Dictionary of structured captions and lead to an answer with a green ✓. The eye goes first to the colorful frame strip, then to the red ✗ marks and the green ✓.
caption: \textbf{Conceptual comparison between prior memory-based SVU and \methodname{}.} Prior methods preserve streaming history as agentic memory [ref], pruned tokens [ref], or KV-memory recall [ref], but rely on a single evidence-access path and do not ensure that retained evidence remains query-recoverable. In contrast, \methodname{} plans whether each query should be grounded in the past, current scene, or future, and accesses a structured Time Dictionary accordingly.
abstract: Streaming video understanding (SVU) requires models to answer user queries over continuously evolving video streams. Unlike offline video QA, SVU must handle queries whose evidence may lie in the past, appear in the current scene, or emerge only after future observations. Existing streaming video systems often rely on compact visual memories or fixed evidence-access schemes, which can lose fine-grained details and fail to adapt the answering process to the temporal intent of each query. In this paper, we propose TimeTraveler, a streaming VQA framework that performs temporal strategy planning with a Time Dictionary. Inspired by the need to search across different temporal regions of a stream, TimeTraveler stores each observed moment as a timestamp-indexed structured caption and uses this dictionary as an explicit source of queryable evidence. Given a query, TimeTraveler determines whether to recall past evidence, read the present context, or wait for future observations, and then applies a strategy-specific evidence acquisition process. Comparative experiments on streaming video QA benchmarks show that TimeTraveler improves streaming question answering by preserving fine-grained temporal evidence and selecting the appropriate temporal strategy for each query. The project page is available at https://geppa.github.io/TimeTraveler.
